query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In-situ reactive infiltration of a minor aluminum-rich alloy into the surface defects of a CrB-based boride coating will form a continuous, dense intermetallic barrier that dramatically impedes molten aluminum corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: A CrB-based boride coating on hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment components that exhibits inherent surface porosities and microdefects.
generation.intervention: Perform reactive infiltration by applying a minor aluminum-rich alloy to the coating surface under controlled conditions.
generation.conditions: The infiltration is conducted in an inert argon atmosphere at approximately 650°C, a temperature high enough to promote reactive wetting but below the full melting point of aluminum.
generation.structural_mediator: The reaction between the infiltrated aluminum-rich alloy and the boride surface produces a continuous intermetallic layer (e.g., an Al3X-type phase, where X is a refractory element from the boride) that fills surface porosities and seals potential corrosion pathways.
generation.mechanism: The localized reaction forms a thermodynamically stable barrier that reduces the exposure of the vulnerable boride phases to molten aluminum. This barrier limits diffusion and chemical attack, thereby reducing the corrosion rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: An improvement in molten aluminum corrosion resistance of roughly 35%, as demonstrated by reduced weight loss and slower corrosion front propagation compared to untreated CrB-based components.
generation.baseline: CrB-based boride coating components without the reactive infiltration treatment.
generation.boundary: The protection remains effective as long as the processing conditions (argon atmosphere and temperature around 650°C) are maintained; deviations such as significantly higher temperatures or incomplete infiltration may compromise barrier formation.
generation.uncertainty: The actual magnitude of improvement may vary depending on the uniformity of the infiltration, exact alloy composition, and processing reproducibility.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrB-based boride coated samples. Treat one set with the reactive infiltration process under the specified conditions, while keeping the other set as untreated controls. Expose both sets to molten aluminum environments under identical test conditions.
measurements: Weight loss measurements after a defined exposure time
Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) to assess corrosion front propagation and intermetallic layer formation
X-ray Diffraction (XRD) analysis to verify the formation of the intended intermetallic phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not exhibit at least a 35% reduction in corrosion indicators (e.g., weight loss or corrosion front penetration) compared to controls, or if the intended intermetallic layer is not detected, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr2O3), alumina (Al2O3) or silica (SiO2) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation. However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components,. The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

proposals.intervention: Disperse fine Y2O3 nanoparticles into the boride matrix via liquid‐phase mixing prior to consolidation
proposals.conditions: Consolidation at ~800°C and exposure to molten aluminum at typical plating temperatures (~700°C)
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation of a secondary, well-adhered Y-Al-O (alumina) phase at the boride/molt aluminum interface
proposals.mechanism: The Y2O3 nanoparticles act as reactive sites that, upon interaction with trace aluminum, form a continuous, dense alumina scale that impedes aluminum ingress and suppresses further corrosion
proposals.predicted_outcome: A measurable reduction (e.g., >30% decrease) in corrosion rate compared to an undoped TiB2 baseline, enabling longer component lifetime
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: Introducing rare-earth oxide dispersoids in the boride can provide a self-forming protective barrier against molten aluminum corrosion, directly targeting the interfacial reaction responsible for degradation

proposals.intervention: Laser-clad a thin, Y–Hf co-doped high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating onto the boride substrate
proposals.conditions: Deposition under controlled atmosphere with subsequent heat treatment at ~900°C (e.g., 10 h dwell) to stabilize the coating structure
proposals.structural_mediator: Development of an interfacial Al-rich bonding layer and well-distributed protective phases within the HEA coating
proposals.mechanism: Y and Hf dopants promote the in-situ formation of adherent oxide phases that resist molten aluminum attack by reducing spallation and interfacial degradation
proposals.predicted_outcome: An improvement in resistance to molten aluminum corrosion quantified by a significant reduction (e.g., ~40% lower spallation area or weight loss) relative to untreated boride components
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This single intervention integrates surface alloying via laser cladding with specific rare-earth doping to yield a protective coating that has demonstrated enhanced high-temperature corrosion resistance in similar systems

proposals.material_system: Conventional boride-based composite (e.g., a TiB2-based system)
proposals.intervention: Implement a thermomechanical processing route using severe plastic deformation followed by controlled annealing to refine and engineer the grain boundaries
proposals.conditions: Deform at room temperature with high strain rates and anneal at ~750°C to achieve a nanostructured, low-energy grain boundary configuration
proposals.structural_mediator: A refined microstructure with reduced high-energy grain boundary fractions and more equilibrium grain boundary orientations
proposals.mechanism: Lower energy, more coherent grain boundaries reduce fast diffusion paths for molten aluminum, thereby minimizing penetration and dissolution at the interface
proposals.predicted_outcome: A reduction in corrosion penetration depth by approximately 25% compared to a coarse-grained, conventionally processed baseline, prolonging component service life
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By targeting the microstructural features that facilitate molten aluminum attack, this intervention specifically limits the diffusion-mediated corrosion processes at grain boundaries

proposals.material_system: CrB-based boride coating on hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment components
proposals.intervention: Conduct an in-situ reactive infiltration of a minor aluminum-rich alloy into surface defects and porosities to form a continuous, protective intermetallic barrier layer
proposals.conditions: Perform the infiltration in a controlled argon atmosphere at ~650°C, below the full melting point of aluminum but high enough for reactive wetting
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation of an in-situ, dense intermetallic layer (such as an Al3X type phase where X is a refractory element from the boride) that occupies surface porosity and seals potential corrosion pathways
proposals.mechanism: The infused alloy reacts locally with the boride surface to produce a thermodynamically stable barrier phase that resists further attack by molten aluminum through reduced reactivity and limited diffusion kinetics
proposals.predicted_outcome: An enhancement in molten aluminum corrosion resistance by approximately 35%, evidenced by reduced weight loss and diminished corrosion front propagation compared to untreated surfaces
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This single intervention creates an engineered, in-situ barrier that directly addresses the molten aluminum attack by chemically and structurally passivating vulnerable regions of the boride-based component

decision.rationale: Candidate A directly addresses the molten-aluminum corrosion issue for boride-based components by proposing an in-situ reactive infiltration that forms an intermetallic barrier phase to seal surface defects. This intervention specifically targets and blocks the corrosion pathways with a single processing step, and its predicted ~35% improvement is supported by evidence on interfacial reaction mechanisms in similar high-temperature environments. Its simplicity, direct action on surface porosity, and clear mechanism make it the best candidate.
